d: Type I: reject true $H_0$ (≤ α). Type II: keep false $H_0$ (β). Power $1-\beta\approx\Phi(\delta\sqrt n/\sigma-z_{1-\alpha/2})$.
80% power at 5%: $n\approx(2.8\sigma/\delta)^2$. Annual SR 0.5 → ≈31 years.
$t$ grows like $\sqrt n$; size decides whether costs are covered. Daily cost ≈ turnover × 2 sides × cost per side.
FWER $=P(V\ge1)$. Bonferroni: reject if $p_i\le\alpha/m$. For $m$ independent nulls, $P(\text{some }p\le\alpha)=1-(1-\alpha)^m$.
FDR $=E[V/\max(R,1)]$. BH: largest $k$ with $p_{(k)}\le kq/m$; reject $1..k$.
$|t|=3$: $p\approx0.0027$ for one test. 100 tries: 24% chance of a false $|t|\ge3$; Bonferroni bar ≈3.5.
Unbiased: linearity, random sampling, no perfect collinearity, $E(u\mid X)=0$.
Usual variance / BLUE: + homoskedastic, uncorrelated errors. Exact $t$: + normal errors (dropped in large samples).
$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma_i^2/SST_x^2$. Fix: White SE, or WLS.
Unbiased under strict exogeneity; usual SE omits $\sum\rho^jx_tx_{t+j}$ terms. Fix: Newey-West, lag ≥ overlap; non-overlapping samples.
Short-regression slope $\to\beta_1+\beta_2\,\mathrm{Cov}(x_1,x_2)/\mathrm{Var}(x_1)$; needs both $\beta_2\ne0$ and correlation.
Correlate residuals after regressing both on controls. One control: $\frac{\rho_{xy}-\rho_{xz}\rho_{yz}}{\sqrt{(1-\rho_{xz}^2)(1-\rho_{yz}^2)}}$.
$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)=\sigma^2/[SST_j(1-R_j^2)]$, VIF $=1/(1-R_j^2)$. Sums of coefficients are well identified; splits are not.
Noise: $E[R^2]\approx k/(n-1)$. $R^2_{OOS}=1-\sum(r-\hat r)^2/\sum(r-\bar r)^2$ against the historical mean.
One signal: $R^2=IC^2$; $IR\approx IC\sqrt{BR}$.
Penalties $\lambda\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2$, $\lambda\lVert\beta\rVert_1$; tune $\lambda$ with time-ordered CV inside training data.
Plug-in: resample from $\hat F_n$. Fails with dependence: AR(1) mean variance factor $\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}$. Use block bootstrap / resample dates.
TS: $r_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_i^\top f_t+\varepsilon_{it}$ (exposures, pricing errors). CS: $r_{it}=\gamma_{0t}+\lambda_t^\top z_{it}+u_{it}$ (premia).
CS slope = long-short portfolio, weights $\propto z_i-\bar z$.
$\bar\lambda=\frac1T\sum\hat\lambda_t$, SE $=s(\hat\lambda_t)/\sqrt T$; Newey-West if $\hat\lambda_t$ autocorrelated; Shanken for estimated betas; cluster for firm effects.
$d_t=L(e_{A,t})-L(e_{B,t})$; $DM=\bar d/\sqrt{\widehat{LRV}/T}$ with HAC. Nested models: Clark-West. Many models: MCS, reality check, SPA.

cards.q: A two-sided z-test at level $\alpha$ checks whether a mean equals 0; the true effect is $\delta$, noise sd $\sigma$, $n$ observations. (1) Define Type I error, Type II error and power. (2) Write the approximate power. (3) What raises power at fixed $\alpha$? (4) What $n$ gives 80% power at 5%, and what does that mean for a strategy with annual Sharpe 0.5?
pts: (1) Type I: reject a true null (false positive), probability $\le\alpha$. Type II: fail to reject a false null (false negative), probability $\beta$. Power $=1-\beta$.
(2) $$\text{power}\approx\Phi\Big(\frac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma}-z_{1-\alpha/2}\Big)$$
(3) Larger $\delta$, larger $n$, smaller $\sigma$. Lowering $\alpha$ lowers power.

(4) $n\approx\big((z_{0.975}+z_{0.8})\sigma/\delta\big)^2=(2.8\,\sigma/\delta)^2$. Annual Sharpe 0.5: $(2.8/0.5)^2\approx31$ years. Single weak signals are underpowered; lean on breadth, priors and OOS checks.

cards.q: (1) What question does statistical significance answer, and what does economic significance answer? (2) Why can a tiny effect be significant? Use 1 bp a day, 0.2% daily vol, 20 years. (3) Same signal turns over 20% of the book a day at 5 bp per side: is it worth trading? (4) What would you look at besides the t-stat?
pts: (1) Statistical: could the effect be zero? ($t$ = estimate / SE). Economic: is it big enough to matter after costs? (the size of the estimate).
(2) SE shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$: $t=\frac{0.01\%}{0.2\%}\sqrt{5040}\approx3.5$.
(3) Cost $=0.2\times2\times5$ bp $=2$ bp a day > 1 bp gross: net negative.
(4) Effect size, turnover and net returns, capacity, drawdowns, correlation with existing factors. A signal must be both real and worth trading.

cards.q: You test 1,000 candidate signals and 50 have p-values below 5%. (1) What would pure noise produce? (2) What diagnostic would you look at first? (3) Which corrections apply, and what do they control? (4) What must survivors still pass?
pts: (1) Under the null p-values are $U(0,1)$: expect $1000\times5\%=50$, sd $\sqrt{1000\cdot0.05\cdot0.95}\approx6.9$. 50 is exactly the noise level.
(2) The p-value histogram: flat means noise; a spike near 0 means some real signals.
(3) Bonferroni ($p<0.05/1000$) controls the family-wise error rate; Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate and is more powerful.
(4) OOS tests, an economic story, subperiod stability, and not being fifty variants of one factor.

cards.q: $m$ hypotheses are tested with p-values $p_{(1)}\le\dots\le p_{(m)}$. (1) Define FWER and FDR. (2) Give the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure at level $q$. (3) When do you prefer Bonferroni and when BH? (4) What is special about factor research?
pts: (1) FWER $=P(\text{at least one false rejection})$. FDR $=E[V/R]$, false rejections over all rejections (0 if none).
(2) Find the largest $k$ with $p_{(k)}\le\frac{k}{m}q$ and reject hypotheses $1,\dots,k$. FDR $\le q$ under independence (or positive dependence).
(3) Bonferroni when a single false positive is costly; BH when building a pool where a known share of false discoveries is acceptable.
(4) Signals are correlated variants, so tests are dependent and the real number of trials is unclear: record every trial, and expect Bonferroni to be conservative.

cards.q: A predictor has $t=3$ in your backtest. (1) What p-value does that mean for one pre-specified test? (2) What if you searched over 100 independent null signals? (3) List other reasons to reject it. (4) How would you get convincing evidence?
pts: (1) Two-sided $p\approx0.0027$.
(2) $P(\text{some }|t|\ge3)=1-(1-0.0027)^{100}\approx0.24$. Bonferroni for 100 tests at 5% needs $|t|\gtrsim3.5$.

(3) Leakage (point-in-time, restatements, survivorship); unstable across subperiods, sectors or small parameter changes; a known factor in disguise (size, industry, momentum); costs and capacity; overlapping returns inflating $t$.
(4) Pre-specify the test, count all trials, and replicate on untouched data (a new period or market), not more tuning on the same sample.

cards.q: Linear model $y=X\beta+u$. (1) Which assumptions make OLS unbiased? (2) Which extra assumption does the usual variance formula need? (3) Which does the exact t distribution need, and what changes in large samples? (4) What do you do in finance, and which assumption usually fails?
pts: (1) Linear in parameters, random sampling, no perfect collinearity ($X^\top X$ invertible), and zero conditional mean $E(u\mid X)=0$.
(2) Homoskedastic, serially uncorrelated errors: then $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta\mid X)=\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}$ and OLS is BLUE (Gauss-Markov).
(3) Normal errors for exact $t$/$F$ in small samples. In large samples the CLT removes the need for normality, but not for (2).
(4) White or Newey-West standard errors. $E(u\mid X)=0$ is what usually fails: omitted factors and look-ahead bias.

cards.q: Simple regression $y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+u$ with $\mathrm{Var}(u_i\mid x)=\sigma_i^2$ varying across observations. (1) Is OLS biased? (2) What is the true variance of $\hat\beta_1$, and what goes wrong? (3) How do you fix inference?
pts: (1) No: unbiasedness only uses $E(u\mid x)=0$; the variance never enters that proof.

(2) $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid x)=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma_i^2}{SST_x^2}$$ The usual $\sigma^2/SST_x$ is wrong even in large samples, so $t$ and $F$ tests are invalid; OLS is no longer BLUE.
(3) White robust SEs (plug in $\hat u_i^2$ for $\sigma_i^2$), or WLS if you trust a model for the variance.

cards.q: Time-series regression $y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1x_t+u_t$ with $\mathrm{Corr}(u_t,u_{t-k})\ne0$. (1) Where does residual autocorrelation come from? (2) Is OLS biased, and what happens to the usual SE? (3) How do you fix it? (4) What caveat remains?
pts: (1) Omitted dynamics, overlapping return horizons, omitted persistent state variables.
(2) Unbiased under strict exogeneity, but the usual SE drops the cross terms $\sum_t\sum_j\rho^j x_tx_{t+j}$. With both $x$ and $u$ positively autocorrelated it is far too small.
(3) Newey-West (HAC) SEs with lag at least the overlap; non-overlapping data; or model the dynamics.
(4) Newey-West still over-rejects in small samples with very persistent regressors: also check non-overlapping or simulation-based p-values.

cards.q: True model $y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+u$, but you regress $y$ on $x_1$ only. (1) What does the slope converge to? (2) When is there no bias? (3) Give a cross-sectional return example. (4) How do you fix it, and what is the risk of the fix?
pts: (1) $$\tilde\beta_1\to\beta_1+\beta_2\,\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x_1,x_2)}{\mathrm{Var}(x_1)}$$
(2) Bias needs both: $x_2$ matters for $y$ ($\beta_2\ne0$) and $x_2$ is correlated with $x_1$. Sign = sign($\beta_2$) × sign(correlation).
(3) "Low analyst coverage" predicts higher returns, but low-coverage stocks are small caps and size earns a premium: part of the alpha is size exposure. A large $t$ does not fix this.
(4) Control for or neutralise size, sector, beta. Do not over-control: if the signal works through liquidity, controlling for liquidity removes the real effect.

cards.q: (1) Define correlation and partial correlation. (2) Give the formula with one control $z$. (3) A new signal has IC 0.04, correlation 0.6 with momentum, and momentum has IC 0.05: what is its IC net of momentum? (4) What does partial correlation not tell you?
pts: (1) Correlation: linear co-movement. Partial: regress both variables on the controls and correlate the residuals (Frisch-Waugh).
(2) $$\rho_{xy\cdot z}=\frac{\rho_{xy}-\rho_{xz}\rho_{yz}}{\sqrt{(1-\rho_{xz}^2)(1-\rho_{yz}^2)}}$$
(3) $\frac{0.04-0.6\times0.05}{\sqrt{0.64\times0.9975}}\approx0.0125$: most of the 0.04 was momentum.
(4) It removes only linear effects of the controls you chose; it says nothing about causality or whether the residual signal survives costs.

cards.q: OLS under Gauss-Markov; $R_j^2$ is from regressing $x_j$ on the other regressors and $SST_j=\sum_i(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2$. (1) Write $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)$ and the VIF. (2) Compute the VIF when two regressors have correlation 0.95. (3) Why can predictions still be fine? (4) When does it bite, and what are the fixes?
pts: (1) $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)=\frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j\,(1-R_j^2)},\qquad \mathrm{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}$$

(3) The data pin down $\beta_1+\beta_2$ but not the split: many coefficient pairs give nearly the same fitted values (a long valley in the RSS). Fine as long as new data keep the same collinear structure.
(4) Out of sample, when the features decouple. Fixes: ridge, PCA or averaging the group into one feature, and interpret only the group coefficient.

cards.q: (1) Why is in-sample $R^2$ a weak guide? Give its value under pure noise for 20 features and 240 months. (2) What should you use instead? (3) Why can a tiny $R^2$ still be valuable? (4) What do you judge a return model by?
pts: (1) $R^2$ never falls when regressors are added; under pure noise $E[R^2]\approx k/(n-1)=20/239\approx8\%$.
(2) Out-of-sample $R^2$ against the historical-mean forecast: $$R^2_{OOS}=1-\frac{\sum_t(r_t-\hat r_t)^2}{\sum_t(r_t-\bar r_t)^2}$$ It can be negative.

(3) For one linear signal $R^2=IC^2$: IC 0.05 is $R^2=0.25\%$. Fundamental law $IR\approx IC\sqrt{BR}$: 500 stocks monthly, $BR=6000$, theoretical IR $\approx3.9$ (less in practice: bets are correlated, costs).
(4) OOS $R^2$, IC and the net-of-cost Sharpe, not in-sample fit.

cards.q: (1) Write the ridge and lasso objectives. (2) Why do they help in return prediction? (3) How do they treat correlated features? (4) What leakage risk comes with them?
pts: (1) Ridge: $\min_\beta \lVert y-X\beta\rVert^2+\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2$. Lasso: $+\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|$.

(2) They trade a little bias for a large cut in variance; with a tiny signal-to-noise ratio, variance is the dominant error. OLS with many features often has negative OOS $R^2$; shrinkage brings it back near zero or slightly positive.
(3) Ridge spreads weight across correlated features; lasso sets some coefficients exactly to 0 (selection), picking somewhat arbitrarily within a correlated group.
(4) $\lambda$ and the standardisation must be fit on training folds only, with purging if labels overlap.

cards.q: (1) What does the bootstrap do, and when would you use it? (2) Why does the naive bootstrap fail for financial time series? (3) For AR(1) returns with $\rho=0.5$, how wrong is the naive SE of the mean? (4) What do you use instead?
pts: (1) Replace the unknown distribution by the empirical one (mass $1/n$ per observation), resample with replacement, recompute the statistic. Use it when there is no clean formula: SE of a Sharpe ratio, median, max drawdown, a difference of Sharpes.
(2) Resampling single observations assumes i.i.d.; it destroys autocorrelation and volatility clustering.
(3) True $\mathrm{Var}(\bar r)\approx\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}=3\frac{\sigma^2}{n}$, so the naive SE is $\sqrt{1/3}\approx58\%$ of the truth.
(4) Moving-block or stationary bootstrap with blocks longer than the dependence; for panels resample whole dates.

cards.q: Panel of returns $r_{it}$ for assets $i$ and periods $t$. (1) Write the time-series regression and interpret its coefficients. (2) Write the cross-sectional regression and interpret its slope. (3) What portfolio is the cross-sectional slope? (4) Summarise the difference in one line each.
pts: (1) For each asset: $$r_{it}=\alpha_i+\beta_i^\top f_t+\varepsilon_{it}$$ $\beta_i$ = exposure, $\alpha_i$ = pricing error; natural when factors are traded returns (Fama-French).
(2) For each date: $$r_{it}=\gamma_{0t}+\lambda_t^\top z_{it}+u_{it}$$ $\lambda_t$ = return earned per unit of characteristic that period (factor premium).
(3) $\hat\lambda_t=\sum_i w_i r_{it}$ with $w_i=\frac{z_i-\bar z}{\sum_j(z_j-\bar z)^2}$: a long-short portfolio with weights proportional to the demeaned characteristic.
(4) Time series: how sensitive is this asset to the factor? Cross-section: do high-characteristic stocks earn more? Fama-MacBeth runs the cross-section each period and averages.

cards.q: (1) Describe the two Fama-MacBeth steps and the standard error. (2) What does it handle automatically? (3) What problem arises when $\hat\lambda_t$ is autocorrelated? (4) What problems arise when the regressors are estimated betas, or firms have persistent effects?
pts: (1) Each period, cross-sectional regression → $\hat\lambda_t$. Then $\bar\lambda=\frac1T\sum_t\hat\lambda_t$ with SE $=s(\hat\lambda_t)/\sqrt T$.
(2) Same-period cross-sectional correlation: it lives inside each $\hat\lambda_t$. Pooled OLS treating $NT$ observations as independent can overstate $t$ several-fold.
(3) Persistent characteristics or overlapping returns make the simple SE too small: use Newey-West on the $\hat\lambda_t$ series.

(4) Errors-in-variables: estimated betas bias $\lambda$ toward zero and the SE ignores first-stage noise (Shanken correction, portfolio betas). Persistent firm effects are not handled: cluster by firm.

cards.q: Two models A and B produce $h$-step forecasts with errors $e_{A,t}, e_{B,t}$. (1) What do you fix first? (2) Why work with paired loss differentials? (3) Write the DM statistic and say why it needs HAC. (4) What complications remain?
pts: (1) The loss (MSE, MAE, or one tied to use: rank IC, portfolio P&L), and genuinely OOS forecasts from both models on the same rolling or expanding windows.
(2) $d_t=L(e_{A,t})-L(e_{B,t})$: pairing cancels the shocks both models face.
(3) $$DM=\frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{LRV}}(d_t)/T}}\ \approx N(0,1)$$ $h$-step forecasts make $d_t$ at least MA($h-1$), so the long-run variance needs HAC.

(4) Nested models distort DM's null (use Clark-West); tuning on validation data adds uncertainty; many models need a model confidence set or White's reality check / SPA. In practice: test the difference of two IC series with Newey-West.
